papers.abstract: We numerically show that a deep neural network (DNN) can learn macroscopic thermodynamic laws purely from microscopic data. Using molecular dynamics simulations, we generate the data of snapshot images of gas particles undergoing adiabatic processes. We train a DNN to determine the temporal order of input image pairs. We observe that the trained network induces an order relation between states consistent with adiabatic accessibility, satisfying the axioms of thermodynamics. Furthermore, the internal representation learned by the DNN acts as an entropy. These results suggest that machine learning can discover emergent physical laws that are valid at scales far larger than those of the underlying constituents---opening a pathway to data-driven discovery of macroscopic physics.

papers.title: Inducing Sparse Coding and And-Or Grammar from Generator Network
papers.research_question: How can we fuse the sparse coding model and the generator network to obtain an explainable generative model with meaningful hierarchical representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a sparse generative model that combines the generator network and sparse coding, inducing an AND-OR grammar and learning meaningful, explainable hierarchical representations from images.
papers.conclusion: The proposed model naturally combines the generator network and sparse coding model while maintaining their advantages, learning meaningful hierarchical representations.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns meaningful dictionaries at different layers, with bottom-layer kernels capturing primitives like edges and object parts, and top-layer kernels combining these into whole objects.
The sparse activations in the feature maps can be interpreted as coefficients in a sparse coding framework, and the generating process can be described as an AND-OR parsing graph.
The model maintains the advantages of both the generator network (efficient learning and realistic generation) and sparse coding (meaningful basis functions).
papers.abstract: We introduce an explainable generative model by applying sparse operation on the feature maps of the generator network. Meaningful hierarchical representations are obtained using the proposed generative model with sparse activations. The convolutional kernels from the bottom layer to the top layer of the generator network can learn primitives such as edges and colors, object parts, and whole objects layer by layer. From the perspective of the generator network, we propose a method for inducing both sparse coding and the AND-OR grammar for images. Experiments show that our method is capable of learning meaningful and explainable hierarchical representations.

papers.title: Inverting Supervised Representations with Autoregressive Neural Density Models
papers.research_question: How can we invert supervised representations to gain insights into model invariances and estimate the mutual information between inputs and intermediate representations?
papers.core_contribution: Presents a method for inverting supervised representations using autoregressive neural density models to visualize invariances and estimate mutual information between inputs and intermediate representations.
papers.conclusion: The method facilitates visualization of model invariances and provides a scalable quantitative estimate of the amount of information preserved by a network, though density estimation in high dimensions remains challenging.
papers.key_findings:
Inversion model samples show increasing variability from lower to higher layers, indicating loss of input information.
Mutual information bounds decrease through successive layers, with the biggest reduction between CONV1 and CONV2.
Inversion models reveal that global pooling induces translation invariance while preserving style and rotation information, which is not apparent from MSE reconstructions.
Mutual information between inputs and layers initially increases and then decreases during training, supporting the information bottleneck theory.
Overfitted networks retain more mutual information than well-regularized networks, suggesting compression aids generalization.
papers.limitation: Density estimation is challenging in higher dimensions, and we don’t know how well a given model represents the true density.
future_direction: Comparison of representations learned using different optimizers or in different training regimes.
Analysis of the effect of training techniques such as dropout or batch normalization on representation and compression.
Analysis of architectural choices such as residual connections on representation and compression.
papers.abstract: We present a method for feature interpretation that makes use of recent advances in autoregressive density estimation models to invert model representations. We train generative inversion models to express a distribution over input features conditioned on intermediate model representations. Insights into the invariances learned by supervised models can be gained by viewing samples from these inversion models. In addition, we can use these inversion models to estimate the mutual information between a model's inputs and its intermediate representations, thus quantifying the amount of information preserved by the network at different stages. Using this method we examine the types of information preserved at different layers of convolutional neural networks, and explore the invariances induced by different architectural choices. Finally we show that the mutual information between inputs and network layers decreases over the course of training, supporting recent work by Shwartz-Ziv and Tishby (2017) on the information bottleneck theory of deep learning.

papers.title: FuxiTranyu: A Multilingual Large Language Model Trained with Balanced Data
papers.research_question: How to build a multilingual large language model with balanced data to mitigate performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FuxiTranyu, a multilingual LLM trained on balanced data, which shows competitive performance and more consistent multilingual representations compared to existing models.
papers.conclusion: FuxiTranyu is a strong open-source multilingual LLM, and balanced pre-training data is crucial for achieving consistent multilingual representations and performance.
papers.key_findings:
FuxiTranyu outperforms previous multilingual LLMs like BLOOM-7B1 and PolyLM-13B on several multilingual benchmarks.
Balanced pre-training data leads to more consistent multilingual representations across languages.
Neuron analysis reveals that deep layers are more language-specific and the importance of attention and MLP components varies across layers.
Languages with extremely limited resources (e.g., Bengali, Tamil) are allocated fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model achieves high performance on summarization tasks, outperforming baseline models on XL-Sum.
papers.limitation:
Languages with extremely limited resources, such as Bengali and Tamil, are allocated with fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model underperforms in some tasks (e.g., m-ARC, m-MMLU) due to limited training data for English.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated prowess in a wide range of tasks. However, many LLMs exhibit significant performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages. To mitigate this challenge, we present FuxiTranyu, an open-source multilingual LLM, which is designed to satisfy the need of the research community for balanced and high-performing multilingual capabilities. The base model, FuxiTranyu-8B, features 8 billion parameters and is trained from scratch on meticulously balanced multilingual data that contains 600 billion tokens covering 43 natural languages and 16 programming languages. We also develop two instruction-tuned models: FuxiTranyu-8B-SFT which is fine-tuned on a diverse multilingual instruction dataset, and FuxiTranyu-8B-DPO which is further refined with DPO on a preference dataset for enhanced alignment ability. Extensive experiments on a wide range of multilingual benchmarks demonstrate the competitive performance of FuxiTranyu against existing multilingual LLMs, e.g., BLOOM-7B, PolyLM-13B, and Mistral-7B-Instruct. Both neuron and representation interpretability analyses reveal that FuxiTranyu achieves consistent multilingual representations across languages. To promote further research into multilingual LLMs, we release both the base and instruction-tuned FuxiTranyu models together with 58 pre-training checkpoints at HuggingFace (see https://huggingface.co/TJUNLP/FuxiTranyu-8B) and Github (see https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/FuxiTranyu).

papers.title: Can Subnetwork Structure be the Key to Out-of-Distribution Generalization?
papers.research_question: Can models with particular structure avoid being biased towards spurious correlation in out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization? The paper investigates whether subnetworks within biased models can achieve better OOD performance.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that biased models contain unbiased functional subnetworks, proposes the functional lottery ticket hypothesis, and introduces Modular Risk Minimization (MRM) to improve OOD generalization by learning subnetwork structures.
papers.conclusion: Subnetwork structure is a key factor for out-of-distribution generalization, and the proposed Modular Risk Minimization method effectively learns such structures to improve OOD performance.
papers.key_findings:
Even biased models that exploit spurious correlations contain subnetworks that are less susceptible to these shortcuts.
The functional lottery ticket hypothesis: a full network contains a subnetwork that can achieve better OOD performance when trained in isolation.
Modular Risk Minimization (MRM) effectively learns subnetworks that improve OOD generalization and can be combined with other OOD methods.
Sparsity constraints alone are insufficient for OOD generalization; the structure of the subnetwork is key.
MRM and its variants consistently improve OOD performance across multiple biased datasets.
papers.limitation:
The work has not considered data settings where group attribution information is available (e.g., as in Sagawa et al., 2019).
The experiments use a label noise-free setting, which may not reflect scenarios where spurious features have higher correlation than invariant features.
future_direction: Explore combinations of MRM with different loss designs for subnetwork and model learning.
Extend the approach to data settings with group attribution available.
Investigate the relationship between the structure of digit modules and subsets found by methods like 'and mask' under more domains.
papers.abstract: Can models with particular structure avoid being biased towards spurious correlation in out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization? Peters et al. (2016) provides a positive answer for linear cases. In this paper, we use a functional modular probing method to analyze deep model structures under OOD setting. We demonstrate that even in biased models (which focus on spurious correlation) there still exist unbiased functional subnetworks. Furthermore, we articulate and demonstrate the functional lottery ticket hypothesis: full network contains a subnetwork that can achieve better OOD performance. We then propose Modular Risk Minimization to solve the subnetwork selection problem. Our algorithm learns the subnetwork structure from a given dataset, and can be combined with any other OOD regularization methods. Experiments on various OOD generalization tasks corroborate the effectiveness of our method.

papers.title: Controlling the Output of a Generative Model by Latent Feature Vector Shifting
papers.research_question: How to control the output of a generative model by shifting latent vectors to modify semantic features in generated images?
papers.core_contribution: A novel latent feature shifting method for controlled generation of images using StyleGAN3, which outperforms a baseline in adding semantic features like eyeglasses.
papers.conclusion: The latent feature shifting approach was successful in controlling the generation of StyleGAN3, with room for improvement in feature manifestation and entanglement.
papers.key_findings:
The latent feature shifter outperformed the baseline feature axis regression method in adding the eyeglasses feature.
For the male feature, performance was similar to baseline but with fewer unwanted changes.
For the black hair feature, the method was less effective but still outperformed the baseline.
Feature entanglement was observed, e.g., adding eyeglasses sometimes altered gender or age.
The method improved when adding multiple features simultaneously compared to single features.
papers.limitation:
Desired features did not always manifest in some cases.
Feature entanglement occurred, where shifting for one feature introduced unwanted changes.
future_direction: Improve the shifted latent vectors dataset with better balancing and human-based classification.
Use a loss function that penalizes feature entanglement.
papers.abstract: State-of-the-art generative models (e.g. StyleGAN3 [1]) often generate photorealistic images based on vectors sampled from their latent space. However, the ability to control the output is limited. Here we present our novel method for latent vector shifting for controlled output image modification utilizing semantic features of the generated images. In our approach we use a pre-trained model of StyleGAN3 that generates images of realistic human faces in relatively high resolution. We complement the generative model with a convolutional neural network classifier, namely ResNet34, trained to classify the generated images with binary facial features from the CelebA dataset. Our latent feature shifter is a neural network model with a task to shift the latent vectors of a generative model into a specified feature direction. We have trained latent feature shifter for multiple facial features, and outperformed our baseline method in the number of generated images with the desired feature. To train our latent feature shifter neural network, we have designed a dataset of pairs of latent vectors with and without a certain feature. Based on the evaluation, we conclude that our latent feature shifter approach was successful in the controlled generation of the StyleGAN3 generator.

papers.title: PURE: Turning Polysemantic Neurons Into Pure Features by Identifying Relevant Circuits
papers.research_question: Can we find and purify polysemantic neurons? How effective is PURE in disentangling representations compared to other approaches?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PURE, a post-hoc method to disentangle polysemantic neurons into multiple pure virtual neurons by identifying the active circuit for each feature.
papers.conclusion: PURE turns polysemantic neurons into multiple purer virtual neurons by identifying active circuits, resulting in more purified features than activation-based approaches and improving interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic neurons exist in ResNet models and can be disentangled into pure features using circuit identification.
PURE effectively disentangles representations, leading to more interpretable virtual neurons compared to activation-based clustering.
PURE attributions are more aligned with CLIP embedding distances than activations, indicating better neuron-specific disentanglement.
PURE performs close to DINOv2 in terms of cluster separation while being computationally more efficient than DINOv2-based clustering.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation relies on foundational models (CLIP/DINOv2) as proxies for human interpretability, which may not perfectly align with human judgment.
PURE requires a partial backward pass for each neuron, making it computationally more demanding than activation-based methods.
future_direction: Evaluation in controlled settings or using human feedback for interpretability.
Ablation studies on clustering full circuits, different attribution methods, and clustering approaches.
Investigating advantages of purified units for XAI tools like concept-based explanations, concept discovery, probing, or model correction.
papers.abstract: The field of mechanistic interpretability aims to study the role of individual neurons in Deep Neural Networks. Single neurons, however, have the capability to act polysemantically and encode for multiple (unrelated) features, which renders their interpretation difficult. We present a method for disentangling polysemanticity of any Deep Neural Network by decomposing a polysemantic neuron into multiple monosemantic "virtual" neurons. This is achieved by identifying the relevant sub-graph ("circuit") for each "pure" feature. We demonstrate how our approach allows us to find and disentangle various polysemantic units of ResNet models trained on ImageNet. While evaluating feature visualizations using CLIP, our method effectively disentangles representations, improving upon methods based on neuron activations. Our code is available at https://github.com/maxdreyer/PURE.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Do Not Find Canonical Units of Analysis
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can find a canonical set of units of analysis (unique, complete, and atomic features) in language models.
papers.core_contribution: SAEs do not find canonical units of analysis because smaller SAEs are incomplete (missing information) and larger SAEs learn composed, non-atomic features. The choice of SAE dictionary size should be pragmatic.
papers.conclusion: Alternative methods are required for identifying canonical units of analysis, and SAE practitioners should adopt a pragmatic approach to choosing dictionary size for interpretability tasks.
papers.key_findings:
SAE stitching reveals that larger SAEs contain novel latents that improve reconstruction when added to smaller SAEs, indicating smaller SAEs are incomplete.
SAE stitching shows that larger SAEs also contain reconstruction latents similar to those in smaller SAEs, but sometimes composed of multiple smaller latents.
Meta-SAEs can decompose larger SAE latents into interpretable meta-latents, demonstrating that larger SAE latents are not atomic.
Meta-latents are similar to latents found in smaller SAEs, suggesting larger SAE latents are compositions of smaller SAE latents.
The sparsity penalty in SAEs incentivizes the learning of composed features in larger dictionaries, rather than atomic features.
papers.limitation:
The study only examines two language models (GPT-2 Small and Gemma 2 2B) and does not include very large SAEs.
Associating SAE latents with interpretable concepts remains an open problem, and the methods do not identify canonical units nor the optimal dictionary size.
future_direction: Pursue different approaches for identifying canonical units of analysis.
Pragmatically choose SAE dictionary size based on the specific interpretability task.
papers.abstract: A common goal of mechanistic interpretability is to decompose the activations of neural networks into features: interpretable properties of the input computed by the model. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for finding these features in LLMs, and it has been postulated that they can be used to find a \textit{canonical} set of units: a unique and complete list of atomic features. We cast doubt on this belief using two novel techniques: SAE stitching to show they are incomplete, and meta-SAEs to show they are not atomic. SAE stitching involves inserting or swapping latents from a larger SAE into a smaller one. Latents from the larger SAE can be divided into two categories: \emph{novel latents}, which improve performance when added to the smaller SAE, indicating they capture novel information, and \emph{reconstruction latents}, which can replace corresponding latents in the smaller SAE that have similar behavior. The existence of novel features indicates incompleteness of smaller SAEs. Using meta-SAEs -- SAEs trained on the decoder matrix of another SAE -- we find that latents in SAEs often decompose into combinations of latents from a smaller SAE, showing that larger SAE latents are not atomic. The resulting decompositions are often interpretable; e.g. a latent representing ``Einstein'' decomposes into ``scientist'', ``Germany'', and ``famous person''. Even if SAEs do not find canonical units of analysis, they may still be useful tools. We suggest that future research should either pursue different approaches for identifying such units, or pragmatically choose the SAE size suited to their task. We provide an interactive dashboard to explore meta-SAEs: https://metasaes.streamlit.app/

papers.title: Controllable LLM Reasoning via Sparse Autoencoder-Based Steering
papers.research_question: How can we control fine-grained reasoning strategies in Large Reasoning Models using Sparse Autoencoders to overcome concept entanglement and improve reliability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces SAE-Steering, a method that uses Sparse Autoencoders to disentangle and identify strategy-specific features for controlling reasoning strategies in Large Reasoning Models, achieving superior control effectiveness and error correction.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can disentangle strategy-specific features for fine-grained control of reasoning strategies, with SAE-Steering providing an efficient feature identification pipeline that is effective and robust.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-Steering outperforms existing control methods by over 15% in control effectiveness across various reasoning tasks and models.
The identified SAE features generalize from math to science domains, indicating cross-domain applicability.
Logit-based feature recall is more precise than activation-based methods, improving feature selection accuracy.
Strategy-specific features are prevalent in deeper layers of the model, with optimal control effectiveness in middle-to-late layers.
Controlling reasoning strategies can redirect models from erroneous paths, achieving a 7% absolute accuracy improvement in error correction.
papers.limitation:
Only evaluated five representative reasoning strategies
Only demonstrated application in error correction scenarios
Only attempted to correct erroneous paths by enforcing continued reasoning
future_direction: Investigate controlling other reasoning strategies
Explore applying control to a wider range of applications
Explore guiding the LRM at earlier stages or during intermediate steps
papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) exhibit human-like cognitive reasoning strategies (e.g. backtracking, cross-verification) during reasoning process, which improves their performance on complex tasks. Currently, reasoning strategies are autonomously selected by LRMs themselves. However, such autonomous selection often produces inefficient or even erroneous reasoning paths. To make reasoning more reliable and flexible, it is important to develop methods for controlling reasoning strategies. Existing methods struggle to control fine-grained reasoning strategies due to conceptual entanglement in LRMs' hidden states. To address this, we leverage Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to decompose strategy-entangled hidden states into a disentangled feature space. To identify the few strategy-specific features from the vast pool of SAE features, we propose SAE-Steering, an efficient two-stage feature identification pipeline. SAE-Steering first recalls features that amplify the logits of strategy-specific keywords, filtering out over 99\% of features, and then ranks the remaining features by their control effectiveness. Using the identified strategy-specific features as control vectors, SAE-Steering outperforms existing methods by over 15\% in control effectiveness. Furthermore, controlling reasoning strategies can redirect LRMs from erroneous paths to correct ones, achieving a 7\% absolute accuracy improvement.

papers.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Identify Reasoning Features in Language Models?
papers.research_question: How reliably do sparse autoencoder (SAE) features, identified via contrastive methods, capture genuine reasoning processes in language models, as opposed to superficial lexical or stylistic correlates?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoder features identified as 'reasoning features' via contrastive methods are often superficial, triggered by lexical cues or stylistic patterns that co-occur with reasoning, rather than capturing the underlying reasoning process itself.
papers.conclusion: Sparse decompositions can favor low-dimensional correlates that co-occur with reasoning, underscoring the need for falsification when attributing high-level behaviors to individual SAE features.
papers.key_findings:
45–90% of contrastively selected SAE 'reasoning features' are triggered by injecting just a few associated tokens into non-reasoning text.
For remaining context-dependent features, LLM-guided falsification generates non-reasoning false positives and meaning-preserving paraphrases of reasoning traces that suppress activation, decoupling activation from reasoning behavior.
Across 22 configurations spanning multiple model families, layers, and reasoning datasets, no features were found that robustly satisfied the criteria for genuine reasoning behavior.
A theoretical analysis shows sparsity in SAE decoding can bias features towards stable low-dimensional correlates (e.g., lexical cues) over high-dimensional within-behavior variation.
Steering candidate features yielded minimal or slightly degraded performance on reasoning benchmarks, indicating activation changes do not imply representation of reasoning computations.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to the specific models, SAEs, and reasoning datasets analyzed; genuine reasoning features might exist in other settings or require different detection methods.
future_direction: Developing better methods for identifying genuine reasoning features that are robust to superficial confounds.
Exploring whether genuine reasoning is represented in a more distributed manner across many features rather than in individual SAE features.
papers.abstract: We investigate whether sparse autoencoders identify genuine reasoning features in large language models. We first present a stylized theoretical analysis showing that sparsity-regularized decoding favors stable low-dimensional correlates over high-dimensional within-reasoning variation, biasing learned features toward token-level cues. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce a falsification-based evaluation framework that combines causal token injection with LLM-guided counterexample generation to distinguish genuine reasoning features from superficial linguistic correlates. Across 22 configurations spanning multiple model families, layers and datasets, we find that contrastively selected reasoning features are highly sensitive to token interventions, with 45%-90% activating when only a few associated tokens are injected into non-reasoning text. For the remaining features, LLM-guided falsification reliably constructs non-reasoning inputs that instantiate the feature's token-level cues and trigger activation, and meaning-preserving paraphrases of top-activating reasoning traces that suppress it. Steering the highest-ranked features yields no improvements on benchmarks. Overall, our results suggest that when low-dimensional token-level patterns are coupled with high-dimensional reasoning processes, the sparsity bias of SAEs systematically favors low-dimensional linguistic patterns that consistently co-occur with reasoning. Code is available at https://github.com/GeorgeMLP/reasoning-probing.

papers.title: Activation Control for Efficiently Eliciting Long Chain-of-thought Ability of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can the long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning ability in large language models be efficiently elicited by understanding and controlling internal activation mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a training-free activation control method (EELo-CoT) that elicits long chain-of-thought reasoning by amplifying key MLP activations and inserting 'wait' tokens, and a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that trains only a small amplification module and LoRA layers.
papers.conclusion: By identifying and controlling a small set of key activations, the long chain-of-thought ability can be efficiently elicited in LLMs, leading to improved reasoning performance and self-reflection.
papers.key_findings:
Long-CoT related activations are sparse and primarily located in the last few layers of the model.
Amplifying these key activations and inserting 'wait' tokens can induce long CoT reasoning, increasing self-reflection rate and accuracy.
Activation changes around trigger tokens follow predictable patterns (sharp rise then logarithmic decay).
The proposed training-free EELo-CoT method improves accuracy and self-reflection on math and science reasoning benchmarks.
A parameter-efficient fine-tuning method, training only 1.51% of parameters, outperforms LoRA and matches full fine-tuning on some benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
The activation intervention rules are simple and may not capture nuanced activation patterns that require more sophisticated stimulation.
Experiments are limited to models up to 32B parameters and do not extend to ultra-large or mixture-of-experts architectures.
The focus on self-reflection does not disentangle other latent capabilities that may be triggered by long CoT, such as elaboration without verification or memorization.
future_direction: Apply the method to multimodal LLMs (e.g., VLM and Video-LLM).
Test the method on more complex planning tasks (e.g., visual reasoning and GUI operation).
Test the generalizability of the method to non-transformer architectures (e.g., Mamba).
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable reasoning performance, eliciting the long chain-of-thought (CoT) ability in large language models (LLMs) typically requires costly reinforcement learning or supervised fine-tuning on high-quality distilled data. We investigate the internal mechanisms behind this capability and show that a small set of high-impact activations in the last few layers largely governs long-form reasoning attributes, such as output length and self-reflection. By simply amplifying these activations and inserting "wait" tokens, we can invoke the long CoT ability without any training, resulting in significantly increased self-reflection rates and accuracy. Moreover, we find that the activation dynamics follow predictable trajectories, with a sharp rise after special tokens and a subsequent exponential decay. Building on these insights, we introduce a general training-free activation control technique. It leverages a few contrastive examples to identify key activations, and employs simple analytic functions to modulate their values at inference time to elicit long CoTs. Extensive experiments confirm the effectiveness of our method in efficiently eliciting long CoT reasoning in LLMs and improving their performance. Additionally, we propose a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that trains only a last-layer activation amplification module and a few LoRA layers, outperforming full LoRA fine-tuning on reasoning benchmarks with significantly fewer parameters. Our code and data are publicly released.

papers.title: Concept Saliency Maps to Visualize Relevant Features in Deep Generative Models
papers.research_question: How can saliency maps, which are used in supervised learning, be extended to unsupervised generative models to visualize relevant input features for high-level concepts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces concept saliency maps, which extend saliency maps to unsupervised generative models by defining concept scores and concept vectors, and demonstrates their utility on VAEs for image and spatial transcriptomics data.
papers.conclusion: Concept saliency maps generalize saliency maps to generative models and can be a useful tool for exploratory data analysis in unsupervised learning, particularly for visualizing high-level concepts in latent space.
papers.key_findings:
Concept saliency maps can highlight relevant facial features for known attributes (e.g., smiles, hats) in the CelebA dataset.
The method can reveal spatial gene expression patterns in spatial transcriptomics data, highlighting regions corresponding to morphological layers.
Dark regions in images may not be highlighted in saliency maps due to limitations in gradient calculation methods, as demonstrated with black squares.
papers.limitation: Dark regions in images are not highlighted in saliency maps, which is an effect due to the calculation of the gradients and not the concept score.
future_direction: Investigate how darkness impacts saliency maps and develop improved gradient methods or normalization techniques.
Explore functional annotations and other high-level concepts in spatial transcriptomics data to reveal spatial characteristics for certain functions.
Apply the method to other spatial transcriptomics datasets, such as those related to cancer and other medical applications.
Combine spatial transcriptomics with RNA-sequencing and molecular experiments to validate computational results.
Extend the method to non-image data for molecular and biomedical applications.
papers.abstract: Evaluating, explaining, and visualizing high-level concepts in generative models, such as variational autoencoders (VAEs), is challenging in part due to a lack of known prediction classes that are required to generate saliency maps in supervised learning. While saliency maps may help identify relevant features (e.g., pixels) in the input for classification tasks of deep neural networks, similar frameworks are understudied in unsupervised learning. Therefore, we introduce a new method of obtaining saliency maps for latent representations of known or novel high-level concepts, often called concept vectors in generative models. Concept scores, analogous to class scores in classification tasks, are defined as dot products between concept vectors and encoded input data, which can be readily used to compute the gradients. The resulting concept saliency maps are shown to highlight input features deemed important for high-level concepts. Our method is applied to the VAE's latent space of CelebA dataset in which known attributes such as "smiles" and "hats" are used to elucidate relevant facial features. Furthermore, our application to spatial transcriptomic (ST) data of a mouse ol-factory bulb demonstrates the potential of latent representations of morphological layers and molecular features in advancing our understanding of complex biological systems. By extending the popular method of saliency maps to generative models, the proposed concept saliency maps help improve interpretability of latent variable models in deep learning.

papers.title: Uncovering Latent Chain of Thought Vectors in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can steering vectors derived from LM activations induce Chain-of-Thought reasoning without natural language prompting?
papers.core_contribution: Steering vectors derived from contrastive activations can induce Chain-of-Thought reasoning in frozen language models, matching or exceeding the performance of traditional CoT prompting.
papers.conclusion: Steering vector injection can effectively induce Chain-of-Thought reasoning in language models without prompting, suggesting reasoning capabilities are encoded in activation and weight space. The method matches or exceeds CoT prompting performance, with injection timing influencing results.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vector injection induces CoT reasoning without natural language prompts.
The method achieves competitive or superior performance compared to CoT prompting on GSM8k, MMLU, ARC AI2, and AGI Eval benchmarks.
The approach generalizes to unseen data, as shown on the SAT Math section of AGI Eval.
Different injection strategies (single vs. continuous) yield varying performance across benchmarks.
Steered models produce more structured, step-by-step reasoning outputs while retaining natural language fluency.
papers.limitation: Performance varies with injection strategy and may not be optimized.
future_direction: Explore different methods for injecting steering vectors to optimize performance and reliability
Investigate generalization capabilities of steering vectors across different models
Scale up the approach to larger models
papers.abstract: In this work, we examine how targeted perturbations in the activation space of Language Models (LMs) can encode complex reasoning patterns. We inject steering vectors, derived from LM activations, into LMs during inference time and study whether these vectors can induce Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning in LMs without the need for natural language prompting. We demonstrate this approach on Llama3 8B Instruct and Mistral 7B v0.2 Instruct and show that activation-space interventions achieve competitive, if not superior, performance compared to traditional CoT prompting across multiple reasoning benchmarks, including GSM8k, MMLU, AGI Eval, and ARC AI2. These findings suggest that neural network activations can encode reasoning patterns, offering a new application of activation space manipulation as a tool for tuning model behavior.

papers.title: Learning Causal Representations of Single Cells via Sparse Mechanism Shift Modeling
papers.research_question: How can we learn causal representations of single-cell genomics data by modeling perturbations as interventions on latent variables, leveraging the sparse mechanism shift assumption to improve disentanglement, causal target identification, and out-of-domain generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes sVAE+, a Bayesian variant of the sparse VAE for single-cell perturbation data, which models perturbations as stochastic interventions on a sparse subset of latent variables, and demonstrates that it outperforms existing methods in disentanglement, causal target identification, and out-of-domain generalization.
papers.conclusion: Modeling perturbations as interventions with sparse mechanism shift enables learning causal representations that are more interpretable and generalize better, offering a promising approach for single-cell genomics and perturbation biology.
papers.key_findings:
sVAE+ achieves higher disentanglement scores (MCC) compared to VAE, β-VAE, iVAE, and sVAE on simulated data.
sVAE+ better recovers the causal graph (higher precision, recall, F1) of intervention targets in latent space.
sVAE+ improves out-of-domain generalization, yielding lower interventional negative log-likelihood on held-out perturbations.
On real single-cell perturbation datasets, sVAE+ outperforms other methods in transfer learning tasks.
The sparse mechanism shift assumption is beneficial for learning interpretable causal representations from single-cell perturbation data.
papers.limitation:
The sparsity assumption may be limiting due to indirect downstream effects in biological systems, especially as time passes after the initial perturbation.
The model assumes discrete interventions and may not handle time-resolved measurements without extension.
future_direction: Incorporating time-resolved measurements from single-cell perturbation experiments.
Handling non-sparse interactions and feedback mechanisms in biological pathways.
Extending the noise model to more realistic distributions for scRNA-seq data.
papers.abstract: Latent variable models such as the Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE) have become a go-to tool for analyzing biological data, especially in the field of single-cell genomics. One remaining challenge is the interpretability of latent variables as biological processes that define a cell's identity. Outside of biological applications, this problem is commonly referred to as learning disentangled representations. Although several disentanglement-promoting variants of the VAE were introduced, and applied to single-cell genomics data, this task has been shown to be infeasible from independent and identically distributed measurements, without additional structure. Instead, recent methods propose to leverage non-stationary data, as well as the sparse mechanism shift assumption in order to learn disentangled representations with a causal semantic. Here, we extend the application of these methodological advances to the analysis of single-cell genomics data with genetic or chemical perturbations. More precisely, we propose a deep generative model of single-cell gene expression data for which each perturbation is treated as a stochastic intervention targeting an unknown, but sparse, subset of latent variables. We benchmark these methods on simulated single-cell data to evaluate their performance at latent units recovery, causal target identification and out-of-domain generalization. Finally, we apply those approaches to two real-world large-scale gene perturbation data sets and find that models that exploit the sparse mechanism shift hypothesis surpass contemporary methods on a transfer learning task. We implement our new model and benchmarks using the scvi-tools library, and release it as open-source software at https://github.com/Genentech/sVAE.

papers.title: A Toy Model of Universality: Reverse Engineering How Networks Learn Group Operations
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the universality hypothesis: whether different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks, by studying how small neural networks learn to implement group composition.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the group composition via representations (GCR) algorithm and shows that neural networks consistently learn this algorithm when trained on group composition tasks, providing evidence for weak universality (underlying principles exist) but against strong universality (specific circuits vary).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that while there is an underlying algorithm (GCR) that networks learn for group composition, the specific features and circuits are arbitrary, supporting weak universality but not strong universality.
papers.key_findings:
Networks learn the GCR algorithm for group composition, which uses representation theory to compute compositions.
The specific representations (circuits) learned vary across different runs and hyperparameters, indicating that while the algorithm is universal, the implementation is not.
The order in which representations are learned is arbitrary and not consistent across runs.
The network's logits can be approximated as a sum of characters from a sparse set of representations.
Ablations confirm that the identified components are causally important for the task.
papers.limitation: The algorithm does not perfectly explain all logits due to limitations of the architecture (e.g., ReLU activations imperfectly implement matrix multiplication).
future_direction: Extending to other group theoretic tasks such as conjugacy, group actions, and automata.
Studying semigroups (which lack representation theory).
Investigating inductive biases of networks more broadly.
papers.abstract: Universality is a key hypothesis in mechanistic interpretability -- that different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks. In this work, we study the universality hypothesis by examining how small neural networks learn to implement group composition. We present a novel algorithm by which neural networks may implement composition for any finite group via mathematical representation theory. We then show that networks consistently learn this algorithm by reverse engineering model logits and weights, and confirm our understanding using ablations. By studying networks of differing architectures trained on various groups, we find mixed evidence for universality: using our algorithm, we can completely characterize the family of circuits and features that networks learn on this task, but for a given network the precise circuits learned -- as well as the order they develop -- are arbitrary.

papers.title: Engineering Monosemanticity in Toy Models
papers.research_question: How can we engineer monosemanticity in toy models? Specifically, can models be made more monosemantic without increasing loss by steering training to different minima, and how do bias and number of neurons affect monosemanticity?
papers.core_contribution: Models can be made more monosemantic without increasing loss by steering training to minima with moderate negative biases, and increasing the number of neurons per layer increases monosemanticity at the cost of compute.
papers.conclusion: Engineering monosemanticity in toy models is possible via negative biases and wider layers, pointing to future work on robust engineering and understanding polysemantic models.
papers.key_findings:
Models can be made more monosemantic without increasing loss by changing which local minimum training finds.
More monosemantic minima have moderate negative biases, enabling engineering of highly monosemantic models via negative bias initialization and weight decay.
Providing more neurons per layer makes models more monosemantic, albeit at increased computational cost.
In engineered monosemantic models, monosemantic neurons implement a simple algorithm balancing feature recovery against interference, and polysemantic neurons implement a low-rank linear map adjusting confidence.
The conclusions hold for various activation functions and feature frequency distributions.
papers.limitation:
The engineering approach is fragile because it depends on setting a bias weight decay rate that must be slow relative to the rate at which the model learns the task.
Naive introduction of sparsity in model weights results in significant reductions in task performance.
future_direction: Make the bias engineering more robust by tailoring bias decay per neuron or tying it to weight changes, or using regularizers.
Understand the algorithm implemented by highly polysemantic models.
Find ways to reduce compute cost of wider layers without excessive performance degradation.
papers.abstract: In some neural networks, individual neurons correspond to natural ``features'' in the input. Such \emph{monosemantic} neurons are of great help in interpretability studies, as they can be cleanly understood. In this work we report preliminary attempts to engineer monosemanticity in toy models. We find that models can be made more monosemantic without increasing the loss by just changing which local minimum the training process finds. More monosemantic loss minima have moderate negative biases, and we are able to use this fact to engineer highly monosemantic models. We are able to mechanistically interpret these models, including the residual polysemantic neurons, and uncover a simple yet surprising algorithm. Finally, we find that providing models with more neurons per layer makes the models more monosemantic, albeit at increased computational cost. These findings point to a number of new questions and avenues for engineering monosemanticity, which we intend to study these in future work.

papers.title: Low-Complexity Probing via Finding Subnetworks
papers.research_question: Can a subtractive pruning-based probe (subnetwork probing) more faithfully detect linguistic properties encoded in a pre-trained model compared to traditional MLP probes, by being better at finding existing properties and worse at learning tasks on its own?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces subnetwork probing, a pruning-based method that finds a subnetwork within a frozen pre-trained model to perform a linguistic task, demonstrating it is more faithful to the model (higher accuracy on pre-trained, lower on random models) and Pareto-dominates MLP probes in accuracy-complexity tradeoff.
papers.conclusion: Subnetwork probing is a more faithful probing method than existing approaches for understanding what linguistic properties are encoded in pre-trained models, and it enables additional analysis through the subnetworks it discovers.
papers.key_findings:
Subnetwork probing achieves higher accuracy on the pre-trained model and lower accuracy on randomly initialized models compared to an MLP probe, indicating it is better at finding encoded properties and less capable of learning the task independently.
Subnetwork probing Pareto-dominates MLP probing, achieving higher accuracy for any given probe complexity budget.
Analysis of the extracted subnetworks shows that lower-level linguistic tasks (e.g., part-of-speech tagging) are localized in lower layers of the model, reproducing findings from prior work.
future_direction: Applying neuron explainability techniques to the subnetworks discovered by the method.
papers.abstract: The dominant approach in probing neural networks for linguistic properties is to train a new shallow multi-layer perceptron (MLP) on top of the model's internal representations. This approach can detect properties encoded in the model, but at the cost of adding new parameters that may learn the task directly. We instead propose a subtractive pruning-based probe, where we find an existing subnetwork that performs the linguistic task of interest. Compared to an MLP, the subnetwork probe achieves both higher accuracy on pre-trained models and lower accuracy on random models, so it is both better at finding properties of interest and worse at learning on its own. Next, by varying the complexity of each probe, we show that subnetwork probing Pareto-dominates MLP probing in that it achieves higher accuracy given any budget of probe complexity. Finally, we analyze the resulting subnetworks across various tasks to locate where each task is encoded, and we find that lower-level tasks are captured in lower layers, reproducing similar findings in past work.

papers.title: Rewriting a Deep Generative Model
papers.research_question: How can specific semantic and physical rules encoded by a deep generative model be located and modified?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method to rewrite the rules of a deep generative model by treating a convolutional layer as a linear associative memory and performing a constrained weight update to change a specific rule while minimizing interference with other model behaviors.
papers.conclusion: Model rewriting is a feasible approach to editing deep generative models, enabling the creation of novel content by directly manipulating the internal rules of pre-trained networks.
papers.key_findings:
The method can add new objects (e.g., hats on horses, spires on churches) to a model's output distribution.
It can remove undesired features (e.g., watermarks) more effectively than unit ablation methods like GAN Dissection.
It can invert contextual rules (e.g., the relationship between windows and reflections) within a model.
The method outperforms standard fine-tuning and edit transfer algorithms in terms of edit specificity and output realism, as measured by quantitative metrics and user studies.
future_direction: Applying model rewriting techniques to other types of generative models beyond images, such as language models (e.g., GPT-3) and audio synthesis models (e.g., WaveNet).

papers.title: TURBO: The Swiss Knife of Auto-Encoders
papers.research_question: What are the limitations of the Information Bottleneck (IBN) principle for explaining auto-encoding methods, and can a new framework (TURBO) provide a more comprehensive theoretical foundation that generalizes a wider range of models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the TURBO framework, a novel information-theoretic formulation that maximizes mutual information between two data representations, providing a unifying theoretical explanation for a broad family of auto-encoder models (including VAE, GAN, AAE, pix2pix, CycleGAN) where the Information Bottleneck principle falls short.
papers.conclusion: The TURBO framework serves as a powerful and versatile theoretical tool that unifies a wide spectrum of auto-encoding models, offering a richer understanding of data representation and neural network structure beyond the limitations of the Information Bottleneck principle.
papers.key_findings:
The Information Bottleneck (IBN) principle has inherent limitations, particularly when data has multiple relevant representations or when the latent space is physically meaningful rather than a compressed virtual space.
The TURBO framework, based on maximizing mutual information in two directions (direct and reverse paths), generalizes and provides a rigorous interpretation for models like AAE, pix2pix, CycleGAN, and normalizing flows, which the IBN principle struggles to explain.
TURBO's loss function decomposes into reconstruction and distribution matching terms, allowing it to seamlessly handle paired, unpaired, and partially paired data scenarios.
Many well-known models (VAE, GAN, AAE, pix2pix, CycleGAN, Flows) are shown to be special cases of the TURBO framework, each corresponding to a specific subset of its loss terms.
The framework enables new applications, such as linking physically meaningful modalities (e.g., particle momenta to detector responses) and transcoding between different data representations.
papers.abstract: We present a novel information-theoretic framework, termed as TURBO, designed to systematically analyse and generalise auto-encoding methods. We start by examining the principles of information bottleneck and bottleneck-based networks in the auto-encoding setting and identifying their inherent limitations, which become more prominent for data with multiple relevant, physics-related representations. The TURBO framework is then introduced, providing a comprehensive derivation of its core concept consisting of the maximisation of mutual information between various data representations expressed in two directions reflecting the information flows. We illustrate that numerous prevalent neural network models are encompassed within this framework. The paper underscores the insufficiency of the information bottleneck concept in elucidating all such models, thereby establishing TURBO as a preferable theoretical reference. The introduction of TURBO contributes to a richer understanding of data representation and the structure of neural network models, enabling more efficient and versatile applications.

papers.title: Dissecting Role Cognition in Medical LLMs via Neuronal Ablation
papers.research_question: Whether role prompts induce distinct, role-specific cognitive processes in LLMs or merely modify linguistic style.
papers.core_contribution: Role-playing prompts in LLMs do not induce role-specific reasoning pathways; they only affect surface-level linguistic style without altering the core decision-making mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: Role-playing prompts primarily alter language style rather than enabling models to replicate the cognitive processes of real doctors, highlighting the limitations of current methods for building reliable cognitive agents in medical AI.
papers.key_findings:
Role-playing prompts do not significantly improve the medical reasoning accuracy of LLMs across multiple datasets and model scales.
Neuron ablation experiments show similar performance degradation across different roles, indicating a lack of role-specific cognitive pathways.
Representation analysis (CKA, PCA) reveals high similarity and overlapping clusters in hidden states across different roles, showing no hierarchical cognitive differentiation.
Jensen-Shannon Divergence analysis shows role effects are concentrated in early to middle layers and attenuate with depth, not affecting deeper reasoning structures.
Current Prompt-Based Role Playing (PBRP) methods fail to replicate the cognitive complexity and differentiated reasoning strategies of real-world medical professionals.
future_direction: Developing models that go beyond language imitation and incorporate cognitive modeling techniques.
Integrating domain-specific knowledge into the training process and designing systems that can simulate the reasoning strategies of different medical professionals.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have gained significant traction in medical decision support systems, particularly in the context of medical question answering and role-playing simulations. A common practice, Prompt-Based Role Playing (PBRP), instructs models to adopt different clinical roles (e.g., medical students, residents, attending physicians) to simulate varied professional behaviors. However, the impact of such role prompts on model reasoning capabilities remains unclear. This study introduces the RP-Neuron-Activated Evaluation Framework(RPNA) to evaluate whether role prompts induce distinct, role-specific cognitive processes in LLMs or merely modify linguistic style. We test this framework on three medical QA datasets, employing neuron ablation and representation analysis techniques to assess changes in reasoning pathways. Our results demonstrate that role prompts do not significantly enhance the medical reasoning abilities of LLMs. Instead, they primarily affect surface-level linguistic features, with no evidence of distinct reasoning pathways or cognitive differentiation across clinical roles. Despite superficial stylistic changes, the core decision-making mechanisms of LLMs remain uniform across roles, indicating that current PBRP methods fail to replicate the cognitive complexity found in real-world medical practice. This highlights the limitations of role-playing in medical AI and emphasizes the need for models that simulate genuine cognitive processes rather than linguistic imitation.We have released the related code in the following repository:https: //github.com/IAAR-Shanghai/RolePlay_LLMDoctor

papers.title: Interpreting GFlowNets for Drug Discovery: Extracting Actionable Insights for Medicinal Chemistry
papers.research_question: How can interpretability methods be adapted to structured generative models like GFlowNets to provide actionable insights for medicinal chemistry in drug discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an interpretability framework for GFlowNets that reveals how SynFlowNet encodes chemical properties like polarity and lipophilicity, and provides actionable insights for drug discovery through counterfactual saliency and motif analysis.
papers.conclusion: The study extends interpretability tools to GFlowNets, showing that SynFlowNet's internal representations align with chemical intuition, and suggests future directions like multi-objective analysis and direct conditioning on physicochemical properties.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient-based saliency with counterfactual edits identifies atom- and motif-level regions that systematically affect predicted drug-likeness (QED).
Sparse autoencoders applied to SynFlowNet embeddings reveal latent factors that correlate strongly with physicochemical properties such as polarity, lipophilicity, and size.
Motif probes show that functional groups like halogens and aromatic rings are encoded in a linearly decodable manner in the embeddings.
The interpretability framework links model decisions to medicinal chemistry heuristics, enabling actionable insights for molecule design.
The approach demonstrates that GFlowNets can be interpreted using adapted methods from supervised learning, extending interpretability to structured generative policies.
papers.limitation:
Focuses primarily on QED, limiting generalization to multi-objective settings.
Disentanglement methods like sparse autoencoders and motif probes impose simple structure on the latent space, which may not capture complex reward landscapes.
Gradient-based saliency is only applied to the Stop action, missing intermediate decision points.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to multi-objective settings such as synthetic accessibility or binding affinity.
Condition GFlowNets directly on physicochemical properties for more interpretable representations.
Investigate the impact of interpretability tools on downstream molecule design and compare with alternative methods.
papers.abstract: Generative Flow Networks, or GFlowNets, offer a promising framework for molecular design, but their internal decision policies remain opaque. This limits adoption in drug discovery, where chemists require clear and interpretable rationales for proposed structures. We present an interpretability framework for SynFlowNet, a GFlowNet trained on documented chemical reactions and purchasable starting materials that generates both molecules and the synthetic routes that produce them. Our approach integrates three complementary components. Gradient based saliency combined with counterfactual perturbations identifies which atomic environments influence reward and how structural edits change molecular outcomes. Sparse autoencoders reveal axis aligned latent factors that correspond to physicochemical properties such as polarity, lipophilicity, and molecular size. Motif probes show that functional groups including aromatic rings and halogens are explicitly encoded and linearly decodable from the internal embeddings. Together, these results expose the chemical logic inside SynFlowNet and provide actionable and mechanistic insight that supports transparent and controllable molecular design.

papers.title: Efficiently Democratizing Medical LLMs for 50 Languages via a Mixture of Language Family Experts
papers.research_question: How to efficiently adapt medical Large Language Models to many languages, especially low-resource ones, by analyzing internal information flow and using language family experts?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an efficient method to scale medical LLMs to 50 languages via language family experts and a Post-MoE architecture, based on the discovery of the 'Spread Out in the End' information flow mechanism.
papers.conclusion: The proposed Apollo-MoE method efficiently democratizes medical LLMs to 50 languages, demonstrating strong generalization and scalability.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered the 'Spread Out in the End' mechanism in multilingual MoE models: early layers concentrate cross-lingual information flow, later layers exhibit language-specific divergence.
Proposed Post-MoE architecture (MoE only in later layers) improves generalization to low-resource languages.
Introduced language family experts, enabling scaling to many languages without adding parameters.
Hybrid-k routing (language-specific experts with cross-lingual routing) outperforms Top-k and Language-Specific routing.
papers.abstract: Adapting medical Large Language Models to local languages can reduce barriers to accessing healthcare services, but data scarcity remains a significant challenge, particularly for low-resource languages. To address this, we first construct a high-quality medical dataset and conduct analysis to ensure its quality. In order to leverage the generalization capability of multilingual LLMs to efficiently scale to more resource-constrained languages, we explore the internal information flow of LLMs from a multilingual perspective using Mixture of Experts (MoE) modularity. Technically, we propose a novel MoE routing method that employs language-specific experts and cross-lingual routing. Inspired by circuit theory, our routing analysis revealed a Spread Out in the End information flow mechanism: while earlier layers concentrate cross-lingual information flow, the later layers exhibit language-specific divergence. This insight directly led to the development of the Post-MoE architecture, which applies sparse routing only in the later layers while maintaining dense others. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach enhances the generalization of multilingual models to other languages while preserving interpretability. Finally, to efficiently scale the model to 50 languages, we introduce the concept of language family experts, drawing on linguistic priors, which enables scaling the number of languages without adding additional parameters.

papers.title: Letters of the Alphabet: Discovering Natural Feature Sets
papers.research_question: How do hidden layers in a simple neural network represent input features, and how can natural feature sets be derived from the data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates how hidden node activations in a neural network can be visualized to understand feature representation and how natural feature sets can be discovered by grouping similar inputs.
papers.conclusion: The experiments provide a step-by-step blueprint for how neural networks derive natural feature sets from data, offering insights into feature representation in hidden layers.
papers.key_findings:
Hidden nodes in the network activate to specific features like vertical and horizontal bars in letter representations.
Nodes 2 and 5 are activated strongly by most letters, indicating potential overfitting or redundancy.
Natural feature sets group similarly shaped letters, such as A and H, or B, R, and P.
Adding 10% noise did not improve generalization in the natural feature sets experiment.
Heatmap visualizations effectively show which input patterns contribute to hidden node activations.
papers.limitation:
Adding 10% noise did not help the hidden nodes generalize better as expected.
Deciphering and visualizing hidden node activations took a lot of time and explanation.
future_direction: Spend more time formatting visualizations to efficiently display hidden node activations for natural feature sets.
Use algorithms to automatically determine the ideal number of hidden nodes to speed up development.
papers.abstract: Deep learning networks find intricate features in large datasets using the backpropagation algorithm. This algorithm repeatedly adjusts the network connections.' weights and examining the "hidden" nodes behavior between the input and output layer provides better insight into how neural networks create feature representations. Experiments built on each other show that activity differences computed within a layer can guide learning. A simple neural network is used, which includes a data set comprised of the alphabet letters, where each letter forms 81 input nodes comprised of 0 and 1s and a single hidden layer and an output layer. The first experiment explains how the hidden layers in this simple neural network represent the input data's features. The second experiment attempts to reverse-engineer the neural network to find the alphabet's natural feature sets. As the network interprets features, we can understand how it derives the natural feature sets for a given data. This understanding is essential to delve deeper into deep generative models, such as Boltzmann machines. Deep generative models are a class of unsupervised deep learning algorithms. The primary function of deep generative models is to find the natural feature sets for a given data set.

papers.title: From superposition to sparse codes: interpretable representations in neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we relate distributed neural representations back to human-interpretable concepts?
papers.core_contribution: This perspective paper presents a theoretical framework explaining how neural networks encode information in superposition and argues that sparse coding, supported by identifiability theory and compressed sensing, can extract interpretable, sparse features from these distributed representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that neural networks learn linear representations of latent variables and that sparse coding can recover interpretable features, providing a foundation for understanding neural representations in both artificial and biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks encode information in superposition, meaning multiple concepts are linearly combined in a shared representational space.
Identifiability theory shows that neural networks trained for classification recover latent features up to a linear transformation.
Sparse coding methods, such as sparse autoencoders, can extract disentangled, interpretable features from superposed neural representations.
Quantitative interpretability metrics, like psychophysics tasks, are needed to assess the success of feature extraction methods.
The framework bridges insights from theoretical neuroscience, representation learning, and interpretability research.
papers.limitation:
The framework assumes sparse latent variables in Euclidean space, whereas some latent variables (e.g., object pose) may have non-Euclidean topology, and the linear representation hypothesis may only hold approximately in such cases.
Practical recovery of sparse codes in large-scale models remains challenging, requiring more efficient and scalable sparse coding algorithms.
Interpretability scores based on pairwise human similarity judgments are insufficient as they depend on context, motivating the need for contextualized similarity metrics.
future_direction: Extending the framework to incorporate latent variables with non-Euclidean geometry or discrete structure.
Developing more efficient and scalable sparse coding algorithms for large-scale models.
Addressing the binding problem—how multiple objects and attributes are encoded without losing relational information when representations are summed.
papers.abstract: Understanding how information is represented in neural networks is a fundamental challenge in both neuroscience and artificial intelligence. Despite their nonlinear architectures, recent evidence suggests that neural networks encode features in superposition, meaning that input concepts are linearly overlaid within the network's representations. We present a perspective that explains this phenomenon and provides a foundation for extracting interpretable representations from neural activations. Our theoretical framework consists of three steps: (1) Identifiability theory shows that neural networks trained for classification recover latent features up to a linear transformation. (2) Sparse coding methods can extract disentangled features from these representations by leveraging principles from compressed sensing. (3) Quantitative interpretability metrics provide a means to assess the success of these methods, ensuring that extracted features align with human-interpretable concepts. By bridging insights from theoretical neuroscience, representation learning, and interpretability research, we propose an emerging perspective on understanding neural representations in both artificial and biological systems. Our arguments have implications for neural coding theories, AI transparency, and the broader goal of making deep learning models more interpretable.

papers.title: Dictionary Learning Improves Patch-Free Circuit Discovery in Mechanistic Interpretability: A Case Study on Othello-GPT
papers.research_question: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features extracted via sparse dictionary learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a patch-free circuit discovery framework that uses dictionary learning to decompose model activations into monosemantic features and then traces contributions between these features to identify interpretable circuits, avoiding out-of-distribution issues and improving asymptotic complexity compared to patching-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning enables patch-free circuit discovery, providing a macroscopic view of the model's internal information flow and turning microscopic understanding into a more comprehensive one.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully identifies interpretable dictionary features in Othello-GPT, such as current move position, board state, empty cells, and legal move features.
It discovers a local OV circuit that computes board state by combining information from previous moves via specific attention heads.
The QK circuit's attention patterns (e.g., attending to opponent's moves) are implemented through resonance between low-level dictionary feature pairs representing move colors.
Early MLP layers identify flipped pieces by performing an 'and' operation on features representing consecutive moves on a line, with attention heads introducing color information.
papers.limitation:
The dictionary training may have used too small sparsity coefficients, leading to near-perfect reconstruction and about 75% dead neurons in each dictionary.
The QK decomposition only interprets individual attention scores and fails to account for the relative strength introduced by the Softmax normalization across the sequence.
Approximate Direct Contribution (ADC) for MLPs is an approximation that treats part of the activation function input as constant.
Circuit analysis is based on specific inputs and does not claim universal understanding of the model; discovering general motifs is left for future work.
future_direction: Discovering general motifs in Transformers is a central problem left for future work.
Alleviating the dictionary training problem of dead neurons to achieve deeper understanding.
Extending the method to language models, which have sparser features and a more complex world compared to the Othello task.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning has been a rapidly growing technique in mechanistic interpretability to attack superposition and extract more human-understandable features from model activations. We ask a further question based on the extracted more monosemantic features: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features? We propose a circuit discovery framework alternative to activation patching. Our framework suffers less from out-of-distribution and proves to be more efficient in terms of asymptotic complexity. The basic unit in our framework is dictionary features decomposed from all modules writing to the residual stream, including embedding, attention output and MLP output. Starting from any logit, dictionary feature or attention score, we manage to trace down to lower-level dictionary features of all tokens and compute their contribution to these more interpretable and local model behaviors. We dig in a small transformer trained on a synthetic task named Othello and find a number of human-understandable fine-grained circuits inside of it.

papers.title: Exploring the LLM Journey from Cognition to Expression with Linear Representations
papers.research_question: How do cognitive and expressive capabilities develop and interact in large language models across pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from human feedback stages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that cognitive capabilities in LLMs are established during pretraining, while expressive capabilities develop during SFT and RLHF, with cognitive capability setting an upper bound for expressive capability.
papers.conclusion: This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of LLM training processes.
papers.key_findings:
Cognitive capability is primarily established during the pretraining stage, whereas expressive capability develops during SFT and RLHF.
There is a strong statistical correlation between cognitive and expressive capabilities, with cognitive capability acting as an upper bound.
The gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities can be bridged by optimization-free methods such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling.
The vocabulary linear layer plays a crucial role in expressive capability, and its training during SFT/RLHF helps reduce the gap.
Layer-wise analysis reveals a plateau in cognitive capability in deeper layers, indicating redundancy in the model architecture.
future_direction: Exploring additional linear analysis techniques for model analysis and control.
papers.abstract: This paper presents an in-depth examination of the evolution and interplay of cognitive and expressive capabilities in large language models (LLMs), with a specific focus on Baichuan-7B and Baichuan-33B, an advanced bilingual (Chinese and English) LLM series. We define and explore the model's cognitive and expressive capabilities through linear representations across three critical phases: Pretraining, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). Cognitive capability is defined as the quantity and quality of information conveyed by the neuron output vectors within the network, similar to the neural signal processing in human cognition. Expressive capability is defined as the model's capability to produce word-level output. Our findings unveil a sequential development pattern, where cognitive abilities are largely established during Pretraining, whereas expressive abilities predominantly advance during SFT and RLHF. Statistical analyses confirm a significant correlation between the two capabilities, suggesting that cognitive capacity may limit expressive potential. The paper also explores the theoretical underpinnings of these divergent developmental trajectories and their connection to the LLMs' architectural design. Moreover, we evaluate various optimization-independent strategies, such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling, which bridge the gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities. This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of their training processes.

papers.title: The Physics of Data and Tasks: Theories of Locality and Compositionality in Deep Learning
papers.research_question: What is the latent structure of learnable data, and how do neural networks encode and exploit it to achieve generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The thesis develops a theoretical framework showing that locality and compositionality in data and tasks enable deep networks to overcome the curse of dimensionality, and demonstrates that diffusion models learn hierarchical grammars and that task arithmetic in pre-trained models is enabled by weight disentanglement.
papers.conclusion: This thesis proposes that deep learning is effective because it operates on a cascade of compositional structures, from local features to hierarchical representations and modular organization of knowledge in weight space.
papers.key_findings:
Locality in CNNs allows them to overcome the curse of dimensionality by adapting to the spatial scale of the target function.
Diffusion models exhibit a phase transition during generation, revealing the hierarchical compositionality of natural data.
The sample complexity for learning hierarchical grammars scales polynomially with dimension, explaining how diffusion models avoid the curse of dimensionality.
Weight disentanglement in pre-trained models enables task arithmetic and model editing.
Hierarchical learning requires feature learning, not just kernel methods.
papers.limitation: The Random Hierarchy Model, while rich, is still a simplification of natural data.
future_direction: Extending the theory to other generative models (e.g., autoregressive models)
Understanding the emergence of weight disentanglement during pre-training
Scaling laws for hierarchical learning
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success, yet our understanding of how they learn remains limited. These models can learn high-dimensional tasks, which is generally statistically intractable due to the curse of dimensionality.
